office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: Anderson Community Schools serves most of the city of Anderson in Madison County plus Country Club Heights, Edgewood, River Forest, Woodlawn Heights and most of Chesterfield [24]; the district lists 12 schools and centers, including one high school, Anderson High School [25, 26]. A current enrollment figure was not found in fetched sources.
Joe Cronk has been superintendent since March 2020 (interim, then permanent from 2021) and plans to retire effective June 30, 2027 [27].

The board has seven members elected to four-year terms in even-year November elections from South, East and Central districts and at large [28]. Current members are Mandy Webb (president, South), Patrick Hill (vice president, East), Holly Renz (East), Rodney Chamberlain (at large), Martha Green (South), Robert Bookhart (Central) and JoAnna Collette (at large) [28, 29].

Four seats are on the 2026 ballot, matching the state list's four vote-for-1 contests: incumbents JoAnna Collette (at large), Robert Bookhart (Central) and Patrick Hill (East) are running, while Mandy Webb did not file for her South District seat, leaving it open [30, 28].

2026 is the first Indiana election in which school board candidates could declare a party affiliation; in Anderson, two candidates filed as Democrats, one as a Republican and one as an Independent [31, 32].

Budget and referendum: on June 8, 2026 the board voted unanimously to ask voters Nov. 3 to renew the 2018 operating referendum at up to $0.1077 per $100 of assessed value for 2027-2034, raising about $2.9 million a year [33, 26]. The district attributes its shortfall to state property tax caps, inflation and state funding levels and says the renewal alone will not close it [26]; at a Sept. 24, 2026 meeting officials put the deficit at $5.5 million without the referendum and $2.6 million with it [34].

Superintendent contract and search: in September 2025 the board voted 4-3 to extend Cronk's contract through 2026-27 after public comment from supporters and critics, including criticism of test scores [35]; in September 2026 the board reported 699 survey responses and five town halls and said the job posting had closed Sept. 8 [27].
Test scores: ACS's IREAD-3 pass rate fell 3.5% in 2026 results while the statewide pass rate was 88.7%, according to the Herald Bulletin [36].
Meeting access: after complaints about a 4 p.m. special meeting on June 22, 2026, the board adopted an interim policy in July 2026 holding meetings at 6 p.m. unless there is an emergency [37].

The board's leadership vote in January 2026 split 4-3 (Webb, Hill, Green and Renz for Webb; Bookhart, Collette and Chamberlain for Collette), the same alignment as the 2025 contract-extension vote [29, 35].

Forums: no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire was found in fetched sources. A Herald Bulletin columnist reported in September 2026 that several candidates have the support of board member Holly Renz and that social media posts have urged defeat of the referendum [38].

candidates.summary: Incumbent at-large board member seeking a second term; listed on the state ballot list as Nonpartisan [30, 6].
background: Holds the at-large seat whose term ends in December 2026 [28].
Gave the board's June 8, 2026 presentation on the district's finances and the proposed operating referendum renewal [33].
path_to_ballot: Was among the first candidates to file in May 2026 and did not declare a party [40, 30].

items: In her June 2026 presentation she said the district faces a $6.1 million annual deficit and projected losses of at least $23.8 million over eight years, including at least $11 million from state property tax reductions and at least $12.8 million from required charter school revenue sharing [33].

Said of the referendum: “The referendum is not a magic fix. It’s not a blank check, and it’s not a way to avoid hard decisions. It’s one part of a responsible plan to keep current local support in place, while this district also has to make reductions.” [33]

In July 2026 she said a June 22 special meeting was needed to fill principal vacancies so appointees could prepare for the school year; the board then unanimously adopted an interim policy holding meetings at 6 p.m. unless there is an emergency [37].

on_incumbent: In August 2025 she moved to postpone a vote on Superintendent Joe Cronk's contract, citing the need for more time to consider public comments [41].
Voted against the one-year extension of Cronk's contract, which passed 4-3 in September 2025 [35].
Received three votes for board president in January 2026; the board elected Mandy Webb 4-3 [29].

candidates.summary: Challenger to incumbent Patrick Hill in the East District; ran for the board in 2024; listed on the state ballot list as Nonpartisan [6, 30, 42].
background: In 2022 he co-led a citizens committee urging ACS to apply for a federal Next Generation School Improvement Grant; the Herald Bulletin then described him as a frequent critic of the district [43, 44].
Ran unsuccessfully for the East District seat held by Holly Renz in 2024 [42, 29].
Said in 2024, “I’m a product of ACS.” [45]
path_to_ballot: Filed by the June 18, 2026 deadline without declaring a party [30].

items: In his 2024 campaign he expressed concern about ACS ILEARN scores, saying, “If you do not accept your failure, how do you know how to fix it?” and that he wanted teachers “given the tools to be successful” [42].
In 2024 he said ACS had lost 1,000 students since 2018 and that the district should report why families leave and adjust to retain them [45].
In June 2022 he emailed the board and superintendent proposing a meeting of administrators, board members, union representatives and educators to plan for the next round of grants [44].

on_incumbent: In 2024 he said change starts with the school board, which must ensure everyone is treated fairly and equally [45].
endorsements_finance: Did not file a campaign finance report in the 2024 race, according to the Herald Bulletin [46].
No 2026 finance report or endorsements were found.
